resources.string: Apps from Modern Apps, F-Droid and the Play Store, in one place.
Search above, or sync your sources to fill this up.
Play Store apps are checked separately. Tap Check Play to look.
%1$s will be removed. You can install it again any time.
Uninstall %1$s? You can install it again any time.
Add F-Droid compatible repos. Apps available on F-Droid are marked F-Droid, others Play Store.
These three sources are built in and cannot be changed. Other F-Droid repos just hand out binaries someone else built, so there is nothing to check them against.
Apps built for anything older than API %1$d are not listed, and are turned away at install even if the listing said otherwise. Old apps skip the sandbox and permission rules newer Android enforces.
Every download has its signature checked. A file with no valid signature never gets installed.
The app has to be the one you asked for
The name inside the downloaded file must match the app you tapped install on.
An update has to be signed by the same key as the copy you already have, or a key that one was rotated to. Anything else is refused.
Some apps arrive as several files. All of them must be signed by the same key, so a swapped part cannot slip in with the real ones.
Everything is checked before the download reaches the system installer. Rejected files are deleted.
A failed check blocks, a missing one warns
If a check fails, the install stops. If a source publishes nothing to check against, the app installs but is marked unverified.
Nothing else on your phone can quietly replace an app you installed here.
The three sources below are built in and you cannot add more. Nothing above could be promised for a repo you added yourself.
Made by the same developer as this store, and signed with the same key this app is signed with.
Someone would need the developer\'s signing key and their GitHub account, both at once.
Signed by this app\'s own key, read straight from your phone at install time
The file matches the hash published with the release on GitHub
One key, one person holding it, and nobody else rebuilding the source to confirm the app matches it.
F-Droid built it from public source code, and a second machine rebuilt it and got an identical file.
Someone would need F-Droid\'s index signing key and their servers, both at once.
F-Droid\'s app list is signed, and checked against a key built into this store
Every entry in that list is chained back to the signature
F-Droid\'s second build server rebuilt this exact version and got the same file
The hash and the signing key both come from the signed list
F-Droid holds the key here, not the developer. A version only shows up once it has been rebuilt, which can take days or weeks, security fixes included.
Comes from Google, who also signs it. Nothing in it shows who actually wrote the app.
Someone would need Google\'s app servers.
Each downloaded file matches the hash Google sent with it
Signed by the key Google lists for this app
The app\'s publisher stamp is saved the first time you install it, and has to stay the same afterwards
No source code, no second build, no publisher key. These checks catch a tampered download or a swapped publisher, but not a bad update that Google signs itself.
Every app here gets a tier, based on how much of its download this phone can check for itself. It says who is able to send you code, not how good the app is.
True for every app here, wherever it came from. Each tier adds its own checks on top.
Who could send you bad code
Tier 1 apps have to be signed by this key. It is read off your phone at install time, so it is always the key this copy of the store was really signed with.
Couldn\'t read this app\'s signing key.
Tap to see what this means
Pinned to this app\'s own signing key
Pinned to F-Droid\'s app list signing key
Nothing to pin: Google holds the signing key
